title: Tanzania Shelves Plan to Pave Highway Through Serengeti After UNESCO Pressure
reason: Multiple independent sources confirm: Tanzania planned a 452-km tarmac highway linking Arusha to Musoma through Serengeti National Park, which conservationists and scientists warned would disrupt the wildebeest migration. A joint UNESCO World Heritage Centre/IUCN monitoring mission (Nov-Dec 2010) examined the project and found it posed a threat to the park's Outstanding Universal Value. At the 2011 World Heritage Committee session in Paris, Tanzania announced it would reconsider and not pave the road through the park, opting instead to build/maintain an unpaved gravel route (approx. 53 km stretch) managed by TANAPA. The paving plan did indeed resurface in later years (2013 elevated highway compromise proposal, 2014 East African Court of Justice ruling against it, and reports as recent as 2026 of Tanzania reviving the tarmac plan). All material details (country, year, actors, mechanism, outcome) check out.

verifications.reason: Multiple independent sources confirm: Tanzania's "North Road" project (452 km Arusha-Musoma tarmac highway) would have cut through Serengeti National Park. A joint UNESCO World Heritage Centre/IUCN monitoring mission visited Nov 29-Dec 8, 2010 and found the EIA showed significant negative impacts (disrupted migration, habitat loss, species threats). At the 35th World Heritage Committee session held at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris in June 2011, Tanzania's minister for natural resources and tourism sent a June 22, 2011 letter confirming the government would not build a tarmac road dissecting the park, and would instead maintain the Kleins Gate-Tabora B stretch (53km) as an unpaved gravel road for tourism/administrative use under TANAPA, while seeking international support for an alternative southern route. This matches the event description on all material points: country (Tanzania), year (2011), the UNESCO/IUCN pressure mechanism, the Paris WHC session, the shelving of the paved plan, the retained gravel-road alternative, and even the detail that the paving plan resurfaced later (corroborated by 2013 "elevated highway compromise" and 2014 East African Court of Justice ruling against the paved highway).

title: Kisutu Courthouse Bombing — Dar es Salaam
reason: Extensive multi-angle searching (direct name searches, alternate phrasings, Swahili-language sources, GTD, U.S. State Dept Country Reports on Terrorism, academic/think-tank PDFs on Tanzania extremism, news archives) turned up no evidence of any bomb explosion at or near the Kisutu courthouse in Dar es Salaam in May 2013 or any other year. What does exist and is well-documented for May 2013 is a different, unrelated attack: a bomb outside St. Joseph's Roman Catholic Church in Arusha on 5 May 2013, which killed 3 and injured 60+, which President Kikwete called 'an act of terrorism' (Arusha, not Dar es Salaam; a church, not a courthouse). Separately, the real Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court in Dar es Salaam is documented as the venue where, starting in July 2014, 17 terrorism suspects (tied to the 2013-14 Arusha bombing wave) were arraigned and tried — but no source describes the court itself being bombed. The event as described appears to conflate the real trial venue (Kisutu court) with a bombing that occurred elsewhere (Arusha church) or did not occur at all. No independent source corroborates a 'Kisutu Courthouse Bombing' in May 2013.
